newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - U.S. expansion may wear thin by late 1998.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - U.S. expansion may wear thin by late 1998.

text.p: Beset by tighter monetary policy and a strong dollar, the long-running U.S. economic expansion may find its endurance tested in 1997, U.S. economists said in the Reuters quarterly U.S. economic survey.
They projected steady deceleration of gross domestic product growth from an annual rate of about 3.6 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996 to below 2.0 percent by mid-1998.
While none of the 30 economists polled on their GDP outlook projected a recession in the next two years, most forecast flagging growth.
"It's largely the business cycle," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at MMS International Inc, echoing the comments of several analysts.
"The economy just eventually runs out of steam."
A combination of factors will drain vitality from the economy over the next eight quarters, survey respondents said.
Chief among those will be the Federal Reserve's return to a program of monetary restraint, said Steve Wood, managing director at BancAmerica Securities Inc.
"I've got 100 basis points of Fed tightening built in between now and year-end," Wood said.
He explained that, while inflation should remain in check, near-term economic growth could worsen central bankers' expectations of future inflation.
"To the extent the economy is still outperforming their desires, we're going to see the Fed finally act on this," Wood said.

A majority of economists in the survey forecast tighter credit in the second or third quarters of 1997. Separately, they projected longer-term interest rates would steadily decline as the economic expansion cools.
That seeming contradiction makes sense, said Donald Ratajczak, director of the Economic Forecasting Center at Georgia State University.

Current levels of long rates "will cause housing, consumer durables and capital spending to slow even a bit more (and that is) probably enough to pull the economy down to its long-term potential," Ratajczak said.
In addition, the dollar should hold much of its ground against other major currencies and that could brake the expansion further, he added.
"With the strong dollar, you're not going to see any gains in exports, so you can take that out of the equation," Ratajczak said.
Although the pundits called for decelerating GDP growth, they were not quite ready to draw the curtain on the economic expansion.
"Unless we get some sort of external shock to the economy, it's hard to see how a recession would unfold, given the excellent balance the economy has at this point," said BancAmerica's Wood.

The health of the consumer will largely dictate the pulse of the economy going forward, since consumer spending makes up at least two-thirds of GDP. The consumer appears to be suitably fit -- confident, but arguably carrying a heavy debt burden, analysts said.

"That issue about the consumer being tapped-out has been way overplayed," said Georgia State's Ratajczak. "What a lot of people have been doing is increasing their leverage because they have a huge amount of gains in their assets."
On Monday, the Conference Board index of consumer confidence hit 116.8, its highest mark for the 1990s.
"For the last three years, capital (spending) has been leading the economy," Ratajczak said. "Now, it will have to rely a little bit more on the consumer."
